title: B2-17 · MSA spoken and code switching

blocks.text: B2-17 · MSA spoken and code switching

In talks, interviews and press conferences the fuṣḥā It doesn't sound like in the news: those who talk improvisingly drop almost all the endings, use the expressions of connection of the speech and pronounce some consonants in the way of their country. And often, in the same speech, passes from fuṣḥā to the dialect and returns: the data in fuṣḥā, the example in dialect, the line in dialect, the conclusion again in fuṣḥā. This passage is called code switching ( ⁧التَّنَاوُبُ اللُّغَوِيُّ⁩ ) and is not a mistake or lack of culture: it is an instrument with precise functions. In this unit learn how the fuṣḥā spoken (G)75), to recognize the signals of the passage to the dialect, to understand its function (G76) and to make it into translation. It is also the first unit of the module B2.4, dedicated to oral variation and production. Three weeks, while EGY concludes-18.

blocks.text: Materials This unit, Reference Grammar (G)75, G76), talk shows and authentic interviews chosen by the tutor, a recorder, sessions with the tutor
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. describe the differences between fuṣḥā read and fuṣḥā spoken (disclaimers, tanwīn, numbers, pronunciation, expressions of connection);
2. speak yourself in a fuṣḥā natural spoken, without unnecessary endings but with proper internal vowels;
3. recognizing in a speech the passage between fuṣḥā and dialect through ten signals;
4. explain the function of each step (given, example, bar, emotion, quote, conclusion);
5. translating a speech with code switching, making the log change and annotating it when It's okay, it's okay. Three-week plan.

The one who switches. All: ministers, professors, journalists, imams, footballers. The more formal the context, the longer the lines are fuṣḥā; The more personal and emotional, the more space the dialect takes. An intervention all in fuṣḥā read, in a talk show, sounds stiff; One all in dialect, in a press conference, sounds unserious.
How do you understand that the speaker has gone to the dialect? Just a few grammatical words (the complete table of varieties is in G77; the origin of the speakers is the theme of B2-21).

blocks.text: Is one signal enough? Often yes: a ⁧مش⁩ or a ⁧ده⁩ in a sentence indicates the passage. But beware of ⁧يعني⁩ , ⁧اللي⁩ and ⁧بس⁩ , which you also feel in fuṣḥā Talked: alone is not enough.

Three registers, the same content. Read the same sentence in three ways and register: 1) as a news bulletin, with all the desinences: ⁧اِرْتَفَعَ مُعَدَّلُ التَّضَخُّمِ إِلَى خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ فِي المِئَةِ⁩ ; 2) as in a debate, in fuṣḥā Talked: irtafaʿ muʿaddal at-taḍaḫḫum ila ḫamsat ʿašar f l-miʾa; 3) as an Egyptian coffee: il-asʿār ġilyit awi, it-taḍaḫḫum baʾa ḫamasṭāšar fi l-miyya. In the second register, the tanwīn of šukran and ṭabʿan, šadda and internal vowels; in the third, the Egyptian sounds (EGY-18).
